overview: This week's papers cluster around how memory and attention are shaped by structure and by the limits of processing. Two memory studies show that later events can reshape what is retained: threat conditioning retroactively improved 24-hour recognition of the starting category in a sequence that ended in a shock-predictive category, and EEG evidence linked temporally guided attention shifts in working memory to long-term forgetting of the deprioritized item. A third memory study found that highly memorable images lose accuracy under short retrieval deadlines just as low-memorability images do, which favors a resource-dependent account over a resilience account. On the development side, children aged 9-10 showed independence between stability and flexibility rather than a trade-off, and successor knowledge, not approximate-magnitude mappings, predicted understanding of the later-greater principle. Two results stand out for the gap between model or normative predictions and human behavior: language models of varying architecture and size underestimated the human integration cost of long-distance subject-verb dependencies in a large self-paced reading dataset, and participants in the counterfactual decision study were far from optimal because of faulty inference, a weakness that statistical expertise did not remedy. A recurrent network account of perceptual grouping in natural scenes rounds out the set, with dynamics that predicted human reaction times.

papers.title: Aversive learning retroactively modulates neutral episodic memories structured by prior knowledge of predictive sequences
papers.authors: Blazej M. Baczkowski, Arno Villringer
papers.summary: Young adults learned two deterministic category sequences (A->B->C, D->E->F), incidentally encoded trial-unique exemplars during sequence viewing, then underwent threat conditioning in which third-position category C predicted shock and F did not. At 24 hours, when a sequence ended in the shock-predictive category, recognition memory for the starting category (A) was better than for the middle category (B), with no such effect in the control sequence (D, E). The authors conclude that aversive learning can retroactively reshape memory for earlier neutral events when prior sequence knowledge links them to the threat.
papers.abstract: Linking memories of temporally separated neutral and threatening experiences can support later recognition of early warning signals. Yet it remains unclear what cognitive processes might allow the seemingly inconsequential neutral events - encoded in safe contexts and thus prone to forgetting - to nevertheless be preserved in memory well enough to inform future threat predictions. Here, we tested whether Pavlovian threat conditioning retroactively strengthens long-term episodic memory for previously encoded neutral events by leveraging prior knowledge of their predictive relations. Young adults first learned to anticipate the order of semantic categories in two deterministic sequences (A → B → C and D → E → F) through repeated presentation of images depicting category exemplars. They then incidentally encoded trial-unique exemplars from each category during sequence viewing. In a next phase, exemplars from the third-position categories were repeated such that one (C) predicted mild electric shocks, whereas the other (F) was never reinforced, creating a category-level threat association through conditioning. After 24 h, recognition memory for exemplars of categories encoded before conditioning depended on sequence and position: when a sequence ended with a shock-predictive category, memory favored the starting category (A) over the following category (B) - an effect absent in the control categories (D and E). These results suggest that aversive learning can retroactively reshape episodic memories of neutral events when they are scaffolded by prior sequence knowledge, bridging temporal gaps and thereby potentially promoting early threat anticipation.

papers.title: Independent regulation of cognitive stability and flexibility in both intra-task and inter-task contexts among children
papers.authors: Xiang Xu, Weixiao Lv, Jiahui Ma et al.
papers.summary: Across three experiments with 38 adults and 73 children aged 9-10, the study measured stability (consistency effect, Stroop congruency effect) and flexibility (rule-switch costs) within and across tasks. Within a task the results supported a two-dimensional model, and the Stroop congruency effect did not correlate significantly with switch costs across tasks. The authors conclude that stability and flexibility are independent in middle childhood rather than traded off against each other.
papers.abstract: Stability and flexibility are essential components of cognitive control, critical for goal-directed behavior and adaptability, particularly in children. However, the relationship between them is debated; traditional unidimensional models suggest a trade-off relationship, while recent studies propose a two-dimensional perspective emphasizing their independence. Previous research mostly focused on adults, overlooking the rapid development of stability and flexibility in children. The current study recruited 38 adults and 73 healthy children aged 9-10 years to investigate the relationship between stability and flexibility in both intra-task (Experiments 1 and 2) and inter-task (Experiment 3) contexts. Experiments 1 and 2 utilized a rule-switching task with stimulus-response consistency manipulation: switch costs measured flexibility, while the consistency effect assessed stability. Both results of Experiments 1 and 2 supported a two-dimensional model for cognitive stability and flexibility in the intra-task context. Experiment 3 employed the color-word Stroop task to measure cognitive stability (congruency effect), and an inter-task correlational analysis was conducted with the switch costs (flexibility indicator) from Experiment 2. The findings revealed no significant correlation between the Stroop congruency effect and rule-switching costs, indicating independence between stability and flexibility in different task contexts, further supporting the two-dimensional model in the inter-task context. In conclusion, this study supports the independence of cognitive stability and flexibility during middle childhood, demonstrating their ability to coexist at high levels based on task demands. These insights deepen our understanding of cognitive control in children and provide a theoretical foundation for offering developmental guidance and developing effective cognitive training programs.

papers.title: Temporal expectation triggers priority shifts in working memory that lead to forgetting
papers.authors: Ziyi Duan, Ziyao Zhang, Jarrod A. Lewis-Peacock
papers.summary: In an EEG study (N = 20), participants encoded a face and a scene with short and long probe delays, and MVPA tracked neural evidence for each item as attention shifted between them during the delay. Long-term forgetting of the deprioritized item was associated with a marked drop in its neural evidence together with a concurrent rise in evidence for the newly prioritized item. The findings link temporally guided prioritization dynamics in working memory to what is later retained in long-term memory.
papers.abstract: Working memory (WM) flexibly prioritizes task-relevant information over short intervals, serving as a critical gateway to long-term memory (LTM). However, how this dynamic prioritization influences what is ultimately retained in LTM remains unclear. Here, we investigated the long-term consequences of internally guided prioritization shifts within WM. Human participants (N = 20) encoded two items (a face and a scene) associated with short (1 s) and long (4 s) delays, where the face was probed after 1 s or not at all, and the scene was probed after 4 s only if the face was not tested. Using multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) of electroencephalography (EEG) data, we tracked fluctuations in neural representations of both memory items as participants redirected internal attention from one to the other across the delay period. Neural dynamics during reprioritization predicted LTM outcomes for the de-prioritized items. Specifically, forgetting was associated with a marked decrease in neural evidence for the deprioritized item, accompanied by a concurrent increase in neural evidence for the newly prioritized item. These findings demonstrate that temporal expectations shape neural dynamics of prioritization in WM that influence retention in LTM.

papers.title: Memorability under pressure: Memorable images are not resilient to retrieval deadlines.
papers.authors: Guy Sheffi, Tal Makovski
papers.summary: Three recognition experiments (old-new and two-alternative forced-choice) imposed strict response deadlines to test whether high-memorability images resist retrieval time pressure. High-memorability images were remembered better in all conditions, but their performance declined under short deadlines just as it did for low-memorability images. This favors a resource-dependent account over a resilience account, suggesting memorability confers an early processing advantage but no special robustness at retrieval.
papers.abstract: Image memorability denotes the consistent tendency for some images to be better remembered than others. Although often attributed to enhanced encoding and storage, we investigated whether high-memorability images are also retrieved more efficiently. To that end, three experiments introduced time pressure in retrieval by imposing strict response deadlines in old-new (Experiments 1 and 2) and two-alternative forced-choice (Experiment 3) recognition tests. We contrasted two competing hypotheses: the resilience hypothesis, which predicts that the retrieval of high-memorability images is robust enough to withstand retrieval challenges, and a resource-dependent account, which suggests that any retrieval advantage depends on available resources. The results showed that high-memorability images were better remembered than low-memorability images in all conditions. Yet contrary to the resilience hypothesis, high-memorability images were not more resilient to time constraints. Instead, their performance significantly diminished under limited deadlines, similar to that for low-memorability images, consistent with a resource-dependent account. We conclude that the benefits of memorability likely operate as a multistage cascade. Although high-memorability images may benefit from an initial processing head start, this early fluency provides no unique resilience against temporal truncation, leaving their retrieval efficiency resource-dependent. papers.title: One, Two, Three, Four… What's More? Successor Relations, not Mappings to Approximate Magnitudes, Support Learning the Later‐Greater Principle
papers.authors: Urvi Maheshwari, David Barner
papers.summary: Two experiments (N = 60 each) tested whether children's grasp of the "later-greater" principle comes from mapping number words onto approximate magnitudes (ANS) or from knowledge of successor relations between number words. Children used ANS mappings to compare small number words but not larger ones, and successor knowledge, not ANS mappings, predicted later-greater knowledge. The authors conclude that successor relations are implicated in learning the principle.
papers.abstract: As we count up, number words that occur later in our count denote greater quantities. Here, we tested whether children's understanding of this "later-greater" principle originates from associating number words with approximate magnitudes, or if instead it arises from knowledge of successor relations between individual number words. In Experiment 1 (N = 60), we found that children can identify the greater of two small number words (e.g., "six" vs. "ten") based on associative mappings between number words and the ANS but do not rely on such mappings to compare larger numbers (e.g., "twenty-four" vs. "twenty-six"). In Experiment 2 (N = 60), we replicate these findings and show that children's knowledge of successor relations between number words predicts later-greater knowledge, while mappings to the ANS do not. We conclude that children's knowledge of successor relations, but not associative mappings to approximate magnitudes, are implicated in learning the later-greater principle.

papers.title: Recurrent network dynamics explain the time course of perceptual grouping in natural scenes
papers.authors: Sami Mollard, Alekh K. Ashok, Lore Goetschalckx et al.
papers.summary: The authors propose a framework in which recurrent interactions propagate enhanced activity within and between cortical areas, with local boundary signals driving early grouping and top-down feedback about object identity driving later grouping. A brain-inspired recurrent neural network trained to group features in natural images learned to spread enhanced activity across a cued object and its dynamics predicted human reaction times. The work offers a mechanistic account of perceptual grouping in natural scenes and generates testable predictions.
papers.abstract: How the brain groups image elements into coherent objects in natural scenes remains unclear. Existing models for grouping in biological vision rely on simplified stimuli with explicit boundaries and cannot explain human behavior in naturalistic settings. We propose a mechanistic framework in which recurrent interactions propagate enhanced neuronal activity within and between cortical areas. The framework links computational principles, neural circuitry and perceptual psychology. Local boundary signals govern early grouping, whereas later stages integrate top-down feedback carrying information about object identity, grouping features across internal edges into coherent object representations. We instantiated this framework as a brain-inspired recurrent neural network trained to group features in natural images. The network learned to propagate enhanced activity across a cued object's representation, mirroring the brain's perceptual grouping mechanisms. The network's dynamics also predicted human reaction times. The framework links cortical dynamics to human vision and generates testable predictions for neuro-physiological and psychophysical experiments.

papers.title: STRUCTURALCOST: A controlled reading time dataset for modeling human sentence processing difficulty
papers.authors: Nina Nusbaumer, Iria de-Dios-Flores, Corentin Bel et al.
papers.summary: The authors present STRUCTURALCOST, a self-paced reading dataset (475 participants, 40,800 observations) isolating the cost of long-distance subject-verb dependencies. Reading times at the main verb increased with dependency length, driven by syntactic embedding beyond linear distance, replicating an earlier low-powered finding. Language models (n-gram, SSM, transformer) partly reproduced this pattern but underestimated human integration cost regardless of architecture or size, suggesting they capture prediction but not the working-memory-related integration cost.
papers.abstract: We introduce STRUCTURALCOST, a self-paced reading dataset of 475 participants and 40,800 observations isolating the processing cost of long-distance subject-verb dependency resolution. We replicate a low-powered psycholinguistic finding at NLP scale, namely that human reading times at the main verb increase with dependency length, driven by syntactic embedding beyond linear distance. Different language models -- spanning n-gram models, SSMs, and transformers -- partially mirror this graded difficulty profile, yet underestimate the integration cost humans incur, with a gap that persists across architectures and model sizes. This suggests these models capture the predictive component of human processing but not the full integration cost that working memory imposes. STRUCTURALCOST provides data needed to drive progress toward evaluating the cognitive plausibility of language models.

papers.title: Making good decisions with counterfactuals
papers.authors: Ma Ricky, Scott Mueller, Thomas Icard et al.
papers.summary: In three experiments (N = 354), participants decided whether to act using observational and experimental data. Performance was above chance but far from optimal, and feedback including counterfactual outcomes did not improve it. The failure arose at the inference step, as estimates of who would benefit, be harmed or be unaffected were nearly unrelated to normative predictions, though decisions followed coherently from those estimates. Experts in statistics, economics and data science decided better than novices but were no more accurate in counterfactual inference.
papers.abstract: Making a good decision often requires knowing something counterfactual: whether a person would be better off if we acted than if we didn't. Formal work shows how both experimental and observational data ought to be combined to inform good decisions. Here, we ask whether people's intuitions follow this normative standard. In three experiments (N = 354), participants decided whether or not to act based on observational and experimental data. Participants performed better than chance but far from optimally. Trial-by-trial feedback about the consequences of their choices, including what would have happened had they chosen otherwise, didn't improve performance. The breakdown was at the inference step: participants' estimates of whether a person would benefit from the treatment, be harmed by it, or be left unaffected were almost unrelated to normative predictions. Yet, participants' decisions followed coherently from those (incorrect) estimates. Experts in statistics, economics, and data science made better decisions than novices, but their counterfactual inferences were no more accurate. Counterfactual reasoning is critical for making good decisions from experimental and observational data, but its logic doesn't come naturally to people.

papers.title: Individual Differences in Spillover During Naturalistic Reading
papers.authors: Cui Ding, Ethan Gotlieb Wilcox, Lena A. Jäger
papers.summary: Using six naturalistic eye-tracking reading datasets and Bayesian hierarchical models, the authors estimated individual-level spillover effects of preceding-word length, frequency and surprisal, and assessed their cross-context reliability, which was strongest for length and weaker for frequency and surprisal. Low-fluency readers showed greater spillover from length and frequency, while high-fluency readers showed more spillover from surprisal, and spillover related to skipping and regression rates. The results suggest population-level averages can obscure distinct reader profiles.
papers.abstract: Spillover---the influence of previous words on the processing of current words---is widely reported in reading studies, yet population-level findings are mixed. We argue that spillover is neither noise nor a uniform phenomenon; it may reflect systematic individual differences in how processing difficulty carries over across words. We analyze six naturalistic eye-tracking-while-reading datasets and estimate individual-level spillover effects of preceding-word length, frequency, and surprisal using Bayesian hierarchical models. Because studying individual differences requires reliable measurement, we first assess the cross-context reliability of these effects across experimental sessions and reading tasks, operationalized as correlations between individual-level estimates from two measurement contexts. The measured reliability differs across sources and depends on experimental design and signal-to-noise ratio, being strongest for word length and weaker for lexical frequency and surprisal. Crucially, we find that individual differences in spillover vary systematically with reading fluency. Low-fluency readers exhibit greater spillover from low-level lexical properties, such as word length and frequency, whereas high-fluency readers show more pronounced spillover from higher-level contextual difficulty, such as surprisal, which may help explain why population-level spillover findings are mixed. Finally, spillover is related to skipping and regression rates, indicating that some spillover effects may reflect idiosyncratic patterns of gaze behavior. Overall, our findings suggest that population-level effects can obscure divergent reader profiles, motivating theories and models of reading beyond the "average reader".

papers.title: The Emergent Structure of Memory Phenomenology Depends on Whether Memories Are More Episodic or Semantic
papers.authors: Tabatha Blaney-Gale, Jordan Poppenk
papers.summary: A large online sample described memories and completed a new phenomenology questionnaire, and folded bottom-up factor analyses yielded five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory and semantic memory. The structure generalized across recent and remote episodic prompts, but a semantic prompt produced distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory. The results support the link between episodic memory theory and phenomenology, and identify strategic use of semantic knowledge during recall as a separate dimension.
papers.abstract: Phenomenological characteristics are central to theoretical distinctions among modern memory constructs. The scene construction framework proposes that episodic remembering involves the construction of coherent scenes, such that the structure of phenomenology may reflect the engagement of the hippocampus and related regions during recall. However, most phenomenology research relies on instruments with content and scoring schemes that embed theoretical assumptions into their measurements. Here, we explored whether phenomenological characteristics emerge from self-reported memory experiences as anticipated by episodic memory theory. We solicited memories from a large online sample, following each response with a novel questionnaire designed to evaluate the phenomenology of individual memories. We used folded bottom-up factor analyses to examine and validate the global latent factor structure of participants’ memory experiences. Consistent with Tulving’s declarative memory framework, our analyses produced five stable dimensions: imagery, autonoetic consciousness, mental time travel, relational memory, and semantic memory. In order, these dimensions reflect multi-modal perceptual reexperiencing, personal meaning, sense of reliving, detailed spatiotemporal context, and conscious use of semantic knowledge during recall. The semantic memory dimension has no clear predecessor, suggesting the strategic use of general knowledge during recall is a distinct and previously uncharacterized aspect of remembering. This factor structure generalized across memories elicited by recent and remote episodic prompts. However, distinct versions of mental time travel and relational memory emerged in response to the semantic prompt, suggesting these dimensions of memory are context-sensitive rather than fixed. While our findings validate the link between episodic memory and its theorized phenomenological elements, they also invite broader investigation of how phenomenology may vary across different classes of memory.

papers.title: Mapping the Representational Basis of Object-Based Guidance: How Colour Availability Shapes Contributions Across the Hierarchy
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Emanuela Bricolo, Marco A. Petilli
papers.summary: Using fixation data from the Potsdam Eye-Movement Corpus, the authors related object selection to cue-object similarity in several computational spaces (layers of a deep CNN, category-level visual prototypes, and distributional semantic representations) in colour and grayscale scenes. Image-based, category-level visual and semantic information contributed complementarily in both conditions, colour similarity explained only part of this profile, and removing colour changed some image-based associations but largely preserved the overall pattern. The authors conclude that in more naturalistic search, guidance draws on multiple representational levels, with colour playing a limited role.
papers.abstract: Previous research has shown that colour is one of the most robust attributes guiding attention during visual search and can dominate guidance, with its removal prompting substantial reweighting toward alternative features. However, naturalistic object search differs in several respects from the simplified displays and controlled designs typically used to investigate the role of colour: observers often do not know exactly how the target will appear, and even when its colour is preserved, many candidate objects may share that colour, reducing its diagnostic value and increasing the relevance of information that generalises across variations in appearance. Does colour retain the same importance under these more naturalistic conditions, and how does the relative contribution of other guiding information change when colour is unavailable? Here, we introduce a computational approach to characterising the representational basis of object-based guidance in natural scenes across multiple representational levels and examine how this profile depends on colour availability. Using eye-movement data from the Potsdam Eye-Movement Corpus, we related fixation-by-fixation object selection to cue-object similarity across multiple computational representational spaces, including layer-specific image representations from a deep convolutional neural network, category-level visual prototypes derived within the Vision Spaces framework, and distributional semantic representations derived from linguistic and scene-based spatial statistics. Image-based, category-level visual, and semantic information made complementary contributions to object selection in both colour and grayscale scenes, while cue-object colour similarity explained only part of this broader representational profile. Critically, removing colour altered the strength of some image-based associations but left the broader pattern of multilevel representational contributions largely preserved. These findings suggest that, in more naturalistic search scenarios, object-based guidance draws on target-relevant evidence across multiple representational formats and levels, with colour accounting for only a limited part of the information supporting guidance. At the methodological level, the computational framework introduced here allows us to characterise the representational basis of object-based guidance across perceptual and semantic levels and to track how the contributions of these representations vary across experimental conditions.

papers.title: Visual search shifts weight up the visual hierarchy from attentional guidance to verification
papers.authors: Andrea Massironi, Emanuela Bricolo, Marco A. Petilli
papers.summary: Using a deep CNN to estimate target-distractor similarity at different levels of the visual hierarchy, the authors manipulated similarity in a 2AFC search task while recording eye movements. First fixations (guidance) were predicted mainly by low-level similarity, whereas dwell time on distractors (verification) showed a clear shift toward high-level similarity, with the relative weight of high-level similarity nearly doubling. The results suggest that template information is used at different representational depths across search stages.
papers.abstract: When searching for target objects among distractors, observers exploit information contained in the attentional template, a memory representation of target features that supports both search guidance and verification for target selection or distractor rejection. The good-enough framework proposes that, because guidance and verification serve distinct computational goals, the precision of the template varies within a given feature dimension: guidance relies on a coarser, relational code that optimizes the reduction of the search space to candidate target locations, whereas verification relies on a more precise, optimal code for target-identity decisions. However, in searches involving real-world, multidimensional stimuli, it remains unclear whether the representation in the template also varies along the depth of the visual hierarchy, from low-level visual features to more abstract information related to object identity. Here, we used a deep convolutional neural network (DCNN) to estimate target–distractor similarity at different levels of the visual hierarchy. We then manipulated this similarity in a target-present versus target-absent two-alternative forcedchoice (2AFC) task while recording eye movements. Guidance, operationalized as which of the two stimuli was fixated first and modeled as a function of their relative similarity to the target, was predicted primarily by low-level similarity, with a smaller contribution of high-level similarity. Verification, operationalized as dwell time on each distractor and modeled as a function of its similarity to the target, was also predicted by both low and high-level similarity, but showed a clear shift toward high-level similarity relative to guidance. Critically, the relative weight of high-level similarity nearly doubled from guidance to verification. Together, our findings reveal a shift in representational depth up the visual hierarchy. Beyond template precision, representational depth therefore constitutes a further axis along which template information is selectively exploited according to the computational demands of different epochs of visual search.

papers.title: Intrusive and voluntary memory from a single system: A retrieved-context account of selective interference in the trauma-film paradigm
papers.authors: Jordan Gunn, Richard Henson, Emily A Holmes et al.
papers.summary: The authors extend an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model to account for the finding that a film reminder followed by Tetris reduces intrusions but spares voluntary memory. In simulations, task memories compete with film memories cued by shared context, and reproducing the selective pattern required sustained support from a retrieval cue distinguishing film from task material during deliberate recall. This indicates selective interference can arise within a single memory system without separate intrusive and voluntary representations.
papers.abstract: Memory theory must explain why interference can affect deliberate and involuntary remembering differently. Studies using distressing films show that a film reminder followed by an imagery-competing task such as Tetris can reduce later spontaneous memories of the film (intrusions) while leaving voluntary memory relatively intact. This selective interference effect is often interpreted through clinical theories of traumatic memory in which intrusive and voluntary remembering depend on different memory representations. We develop an alternative account in an emotional Context Maintenance and Retrieval (eCMR) model that predicts sequences of film and non-film recall events. Events become associated with context, a changing internal representation of experience. A film reminder reinstates film-associated context, so mental imagery generated during the subsequent task becomes associated with that context. During later retrieval, task memories compete with film memories cued by the same context, reducing film recall without weakening the original film associations. During deliberate recall, however, we propose that people pursue the goal of remembering the film by constructing and maintaining a retrieval cue that distinguishes film from task material. In simulations, sustained support from this cue was required to reproduce the selective-interference pattern across reminder and task conditions, protecting deliberate recall relative to involuntary retrieval. These results suggest that competitor learning and retrieval cueing can produce selective interference within a shared memory system, motivating tests in other memory tasks.

papers.title: Is Guessing to Blame? Comparing Two Accounts of Attenuated Monitoring Accuracy in Recognition-Based Metamemory Judgments
papers.authors: Franziska Magdalene Leipold, Constantin Gregor Meyer-Grant
papers.summary: The authors derived predictions for the manifest correlation between judgments of learning and recognition performance under the two-high-threshold model (which includes guessing) and signal detection theory, and tested them in an experiment manipulating response bias. The two-high-threshold model accounted for the observed difference between conditions with a single latent correlation, while signal detection theory did not. This suggests guessing contaminates the commonly used manifest correlations, and that modeling the process can recover the underlying monitoring accuracy.
papers.abstract: The relative accuracy of prospective metamemory monitoring is typically assessed through the association between judgments of learning (JOLs) and subsequent memory performance. In recognition paradigms, however, manifest correlations can vary across task structures, and prior work insinuated that such differences may reflect guessing processes rather than differences in underlying monitoring ability. We formally derived model-implied predictions for the manifest JOL–recognition correlation under two competing theoretical frameworks: the two-high-threshold model (2HTM), which explicitly allows for guessing, and signal detection theory (SDT), which does not. We tested these predictions in an original experiment that manipulated response bias. The observed difference in the manifest JOL–recognition correlation between conditions was well accounted for by the 2HTM under a single latent correlation, whereas SDT clearly failed to do so. These findings suggest that guessing contaminates manifest correlations commonly used as proxies for monitoring accuracy, and that adequately modeling the underlying process can recover the latent association those proxies are meant to capture.

papers.title: The Limits of Identifiability in the Self-Exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Model
papers.authors: Hannah Pongratz, Constantin Gregor Meyer-Grant
papers.summary: Using asymptotic arguments and extensive simulations, the authors show that under certain conditions key parameters of the self-exciting Ornstein-Uhlenbeck evidence-accumulation model, proposed to capture confirmation bias under speed emphasis, are not jointly identifiable. They explain the cause of the problem, examine its consequences for model-based inference, and suggest ways to resolve or mitigate it. This bears on whether this model can be used to distinguish its account of speed-accuracy tradeoffs from boundary-based accounts.
papers.abstract: Evidence-accumulation models play a central role in the field of decision-making research, offering a comprehensive framework for understanding choice behavior and response times, including speed–accuracy tradeoffs (SATs). In this framework, the dominant explanation for SATs has long been that prioritizing speed lowers the boundary separation, meaning less evidence is needed to make a choice. Recently, however, an alternative account has been proposed according to which emphasizing speed induces a confirmation bias toward the currently favored option. Such a behavior can be formally captured by a self-exciting Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process. However, drawing on asymptotic arguments and extensive simulation studies, we demonstrate that under certain conditions, key parameters of the resulting evidence-accumulation model are not jointly identifiable. We explain the underlying cause of this identifiability issue, examine its practical consequences for model-based inference, andpresent potential strategies to resolve or mitigate it.

papers.title: The Description–Experience Gap in Loss Aversion
papers.authors: Nuno Busch, Thorsten Pachur
papers.summary: The authors tested whether the description–experience gap extends to loss aversion. A meta-reanalysis of raw data from existing studies (88,409 choices; N_Desc = 439, N_Exp = 468) and a preregistered experiment (19,435 choices; N = 202 per group) both found stronger loss aversion, as estimated with cumulative prospect theory, in experience-based than description-based choices. The gap also appeared in an analysis that does not rely on a latent loss aversion parameter, and a reinforcement learning model suggests asymmetric learning from positive versus negative prediction errors during sampling as a possible mechanism.
papers.abstract: Humans make different decisions under risk when they acquire information about their options through experience than when they learn it from a summary description. Research on this description–experience gap has largely focused on differences in probability weighting—for instance, how low-probability events are reflected in people’s decisions. Here, we show that the gap manifests much more broadly and also occurs with regard to the influence of outcomes. Specifically, we investigated how description- and experience-based decisions differ in loss aversion—the tendency for loss outcomes to have a greater impact on choice than equivalent gain outcomes. We first conducted a meta-reanalysis synthesizing raw data of all available datasets that directly compared description- and experience-based decisions involving mixed-domain lotteries (88,409 choices in total across N_Desc = 439 and N_Exp = 468). The results indicate that loss aversion, measured with cumulative prospect theory (CPT), is more pronounced in experience-based than in description-based choices. We then replicated this description–experience gap in loss aversion in a large-scale experiment with preregistered methods (19,435 choices by N_Desc = 202 and N_Exp = 202) tailored to address potential limitations of the studies included in the meta-analysis, and also showed the gap in an analysis that does not depend on estimating a latent loss aversion parameter. An analysis of the experience-based choices with a reinforcement learning model suggests that a possible mechanism for the apparently higher loss aversion in decisions from experience could be asymmetric learning after positive versus negative prediction errors during experiential sampling.

papers.title: Assessing psychological, neural and AI-based representational geometries across multiple similarity properties
papers.authors: Johan Alejandro Gamba, Megan A. K. Peters, Vincent Taschereau-Dumouchel et al.
papers.summary: The study collected pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects across eight properties and used RSA and multidimensional scaling to identify three mental spaces: object features/general similarity, affective evaluation, and color. In an fMRI study with 80 participants, object-feature ratings correlated with representational structure in visual and prefrontal cortices, and affective ratings unexpectedly also correlated with visual cortex patterns. Visual cortices showed higher noise ceilings and more consistent behavioural alignment than associative regions, and AI models that performed well on specific properties correlated with the behavioural and fMRI RSA matrices. The authors conclude that similarity is multidimensional, with neural correspondence depending on content, regional variability and modelling method.
papers.abstract: Assessing similarity between objects is a fundamental cognitive process, and similarity judgments can assess many different attributes, including objective properties (color, shape) or subjective appraisals (preference, scariness). Here, we investigated how psychological similarity across eight different properties relates to neural representational geometries and artificial models. We first collected large-scale pairwise similarity ratings for 280 objects. Using representational similarity analysis (RSA) and multidimensional scaling, we identified three mental representational spaces: one defined by multiple object features and general similarity, a second by affective evaluations, and a third by color. Combining fMRI and RSA in 80 participants, we found that object feature ratings significantly correlated with representational structures in visual and prefrontal cortices. Unexpectedly, affective ratings also correlated with patterns in visual cortices. Crucially, regional variability strongly shaped these correspondences: visual cortices exhibited high noise ceilings and consistent alignment with behavior, whereas associative regions showed greater across-subjects variability and weaker correlations. Finally, algorithms and neural networks with high classification performance on specific properties strongly correlated with behavioral and fMRI RSA matrices. Together, these results demonstrate that similarity is a multidimensional construct that comprises multiple representational spaces whose neural correspondence is shaped by representational content, regional variability, and modeling methodology.

papers.title: Orthographic retrieval unfolds in parallel with single-word production
papers.authors: Jens Roeser, Pablo Aros Muñoz, Markus Damian et al.
papers.summary: Four picture-word interference experiments (Ns = 60, 72, 96, 93) had participants type or speak picture names while ignoring non-word distractors that either matched the target's spelling pattern or offered a phonologically plausible alternative spelling. Mixture-model analyses showed that spelling-mismatch distractors sometimes sped onset but increased the probability of long-duration responses later in time and within typed words, and these late effects were absent for spoken responses. The results challenge the assumption that spelling is fully retrieved before written output begins, suggesting orthographic retrieval remains susceptible to phonological alternatives during writing.
papers.abstract: Written word production is often assumed to begin after the relevant spelling has been retrieved. We challenge this pre-onset assumption by asking whether spelling-related processing can continue during output. Across four picture-word interference experiments (Ns = 60, 72, 96, 93), participants typed or spoke picture names while ignoring pronounceable non-word distractors. Distractors either preserved the target-compatible spelling pattern or introduced a phonologically plausible alternative spelling; only the latter should disrupt writing if phonology makes alternative spellings relevant during orthographic retrieval. Bayesian mixed-effects mixture models estimated the probability that response-onset latencies and post-onset intervals came from a longer-duration component. Spelling-mismatch distractors sometimes facilitated onset responses but increased long-duration probability at later timings and within typed words. These late mismatch effects disappeared for spoken responses. These time-course data challenge the classical assumption that written words are mentally prepared as complete spellings before output begins; instead, orthographic retrieval can remain vulnerable to phonologically plausible alternatives during written production.

papers.title: When attention turns inward: Mind wandering reduces perceptual sensitivity across visual fields
papers.authors: Bianca de Haan
papers.summary: In a preregistered online signal detection task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task while detecting stimuli in the left and right visual fields. Perceptual sensitivity (d′) was lower on mind-wandering trials, consistent with perceptual decoupling, but the reduction did not differ between visual fields. This suggests decoupling reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing rather than a lateralised one, and that the attentional systems involved may differ from those underlying slower fluctuations such as alertness.
papers.abstract: We all mind wander from time to time, where instead of being focussed on our task, we start thinking about task-unrelated personal events or concerns. In daily life, however, mind wandering is often associated with reduced processing of external information. This is commonly explained by the decoupling hypothesis, which posits that processing of external sensory information is attenuated when attention turns inward. However, it remains unclear whether perceptual decoupling reflects a global, uniform attenuation of sensory processing, or a spatially-specific reduction linked to lateralised attentional mechanisms. In the current, pre-registered study, we used an online signal detection task to assess the impact of mind wandering on perceptual performance in the left and right visual fields. While performing the task, participants periodically reported whether they were mind wandering or on task. Consistent with the decoupling hypothesis, perceptual sensitivity (d′) was significantly reduced on trials during which participants reported mind wandering compared to on-task trials. However, this reduction in sensitivity did not differ between stimuli presented in the left and right visual field. These findings suggest that perceptual decoupling during mind wandering reflects a global attenuation of sensory processing, and that attentional systems involved during mind wandering may be distinct from those associated with slower fluctuations of attentional resources such as reductions in alertness.

papers.title: First Frequency, then Transitional Probability: Insights from primate statistical learning
papers.summary: Guinea baboons performed a serial reaction time task designed to dissociate the frequency of local sequences from transitional probability (TP), yielding trial-by-trial learning data without the possible use of verbalised rules. Learning was driven mainly by frequency during the first 2,000 trials, with the usual dominance of TP emerging only later. The findings challenge the view that TP is the primary cue in statistical learning and constrain computational models of sequence learning.
papers.abstract: Statistical learning is a fundamental cognitive capacity, whereby humans and other species extract the structure of sequences based on statistical cues. Among these cues, Transitional Probability (TP) quantifies the probability of the next stimulus given the preceding one(s), while Frequency quantifies the relative occurrence of local sequences. Mechanistic explanations have generally considered TP the prevalent cues, but a role of Frequency cannot be ignored. Yet, the specific contributions of each, and their interaction, are not well understood. Here, we report a simple serial reaction time experiment that 1) provides online, trial-by-trial learning data, 2) allows a clear dissociation of Frequency and TP, 3) excludes the involvement of internal verbalized rules by testing non-human primates (Guinea baboons, Papio papio). Our results show that, contrary to the traditional view, Frequency can be the main cue influencing statistical learning. Indeed, we found learning to be primarily determined by Frequency in the first 2,000 trials of the learning phase, while the usual prevalence of TP emerged only later on. These data provide a better understanding of the interactions between statistical factors involved in sequence processing. They also constitute new constraints for computational models of statistical learning and challenge existing results.

papers.title: Non-commitment in mental imagery is distinct from perceptual inattention, and supports hierarchical scene construction
papers.authors: Yichen Li, Veronika Hammond, Tomer David Ullman
papers.summary: Across three experiments (N = 3,895 total), the authors asked whether missing details in mental imagery reflect genuine non-commitment or the same failures to notice, encode or recall that affect perception. Properties left out of imagined scenes did not correlate with those missed in briefly presented real images, and imagery unfolded hierarchically over time: core entities and spatial relations first, then physical properties, then surface details such as color and texture. Attempts to interrupt or constrain construction did not change this order. The authors interpret the results as supporting a hierarchical partial-scene construction account.
papers.abstract: When calling an image before the mind's eye, people often do not include basic properties of the mental scene. For example, when imagining a person knocking a ball off a table, people may neglect to consider the color of the ball. This "non-commitment" in imagery has been part of ongoing debates on the nature of mental imagery in philosophy and cognitive science, but the central question of its origin remains open. It is possible that this lack of detail in the imagination reflects actual non-commitment, as one constructs a hierarchical mental scene. But it is also possible that people do form highly detailed mental images, but fail to notice, encode, or recall properties of the image, for the same reasons that they do not notice, encode, or recall details of real scenes in direct perception. We tested these contrasting hypotheses across three experiments (N=3,895 total). First, we compared non-commitment patterns in mental imagery with the details that participants failed to notice in briefly presented real images. We found no correlation between properties that were non-committed to in the imagination, and those missed under rapid perception, indicating that non-commitment does not simply arise from perceptual noise. Next, we examined the temporal unfolding of mental imagery, and found consistent evidence of a hierarchical pattern: core entities and spatial relations, then physical properties, then surface details like color and texture. Attempts to interrupt or constrain scene construction did not change the hierarchical ordering. We suggest the results support a hierarchical partial-scene construction account of mental imagery.

papers.title: Event segmentation aligns emotional learning and episodic memory
papers.authors: Patrick Laing, Josh Cisler, Joseph E. Dunsmoor
papers.summary: In a preregistered two-day Pavlovian category-conditioning study, category-shock associations reversed across learning phases, with one group receiving an explicit event boundary before each reversal and the other experiencing continuous reversals. At 24 hours, the segmentation group showed selectively enhanced recognition memory for threat-predictive items, whereas the continuous group showed flatter, less selective memory. Learning dynamics during encoding predicted later selective memory, with segmentation shifting this coupling toward the most recent reversal. The results suggest event boundaries help align episodic memory with currently relevant emotional significance.
papers.abstract: Emotion prioritizes not only what was significant, but when it was significant. When temporal structure is insufficient to bind emotional relevance to distinct episodes, emotional experiences can lead to overgeneralization and source confusion. Here, we tested whether event boundaries serve as a control mechanism that allows emotional prioritization in memory to reset and re-bind as relevance changes over time. Participants completed a preregistered two-day Pavlovian category-conditioning in which category-shock associations reversed across multiple learning phases. In one group, each reversal phase was preceded by a brief but explicit event boundary signaling an associative transition; in the other group, reversals occurred continuously without an explicit boundary. Episodic recognition memory for trial-unique conditioned stimuli, tested 24-hours later, showed selective enhancement for threat-predictive items in the segmentation group—most prominently during early and final learning epochs—whereas continuous encoding produced flatter, less selective memory profiles that failed to fully track changing emotional contingencies. Individual differences in learning dynamics during encoding predicted selective episodic memory at 24hrs, with event segmentation shifting this learning-memory coupling to the most recent threat reversal rather than the earliest one. Overall, event boundaries promoted tighter alignment between episodic memory and emotional relevance at the time of experience. These findings suggest that event segmentation supports adaptive memory prioritization by binding emotional significance to what is most relevant in the moment.

papers.title: Charting the ontogeny of mnemonic processes in childhood: the COMIC dataset
papers.authors: Tydings McClary, Elisa Buchberger, Ann-Kathrin Joechner et al.
papers.summary: This data paper presents the COMIC dataset from 180 children aged 4–8 years who completed four memory tasks indexing pattern categorization, pattern separation and pattern completion, plus three standardized intelligence subtests. It also describes a semi-automated data-cleaning pipeline for developmental behavioural data that can serve as a template for handling common data-quality problems in studies with young children. The resource is intended to support research on how generalization and memory specificity develop in early and middle childhood.
papers.abstract: The human memory system balances two complementary functions: generalization, which involves extracting regularities across experiences, and specificity, which involves retaining the unique details of individual events. Understanding how this balance develops can benefit from a neurocomputational perspective in which three core computations, pattern categorization, pattern separation, and pattern completion, differentially support generalization and memory specificity. Guided by this framework, we present a dataset from 180 children aged 4–8 years who completed four age-appropriate memory tasks that provide behavioral indices of these computations. Children additionally completed three standardized intelligence subtests. Alongside the dataset, we describe a semi-automated data-cleaning pipeline designed for developmental behavioral data, which can serve as a template for identifying and resolving common data-quality issues in studies with young children. In sum, this dataset provides a resource for investigating the development of memory computations supporting adaptive functioning across early and middle childhood.

papers.title: Two sides of the same coin in memory: Speech and its accompanying gesture are remembered together
papers.summary: In two experiments (N = 20 and N = 43), participants watched an actor speak sentences with related, unrelated or no gestures, then recognized the sentences and judged whether a gesture had been present or related. Recognition was better after related than unrelated gestures but not better than after no gesture. Gesture judgments were above chance and more accurate for confidently recognized sentences, for which participants also tended to report non-matching gestures as matching. The authors conclude that gesture memory is partly retrieved with the sentence and partly inferred from it, indicating close coupling between speech and gesture memory.
papers.abstract: When a speaker gestures, speech and gesture form one multimodal event. Memory research mostly asks how gestures help people remember speech, not how the gesture is remembered or how the two relate. Participants watched videos of an actor speaking sentences with a related gesture or none (Experiment 1, N = 20), or a related or unrelated gesture (Experiment 2, N = 43). They recognized written sentences and, for each called old, judged whether a gesture had been present (Experiment 1) or related (Experiment 2), with confidence ratings. Recognition was better after related than unrelated gestures, but not better after related gestures than none. Gesture judgments were above chance and more accurate for confidently recognized sentences; for these, participants also tended to report non-matching gestures as matching (Experiment 2). Gesture reports thus appear partly retrieved with the sentence and partly inferred from it: memory for speech and gesture is closely coupled.

papers.title: Unsupervised transfer in relational category learning
papers.authors: Hilary Don, Micah Goldwater, Kit S Double et al.
papers.summary: Participants learned to categorise stimuli by monotonic versus non-monotonic relations among line lengths, via classification or inference learning, and were then tested without feedback on luminance-based dot arrays and digit sequences. Inference learning produced stronger relational responding in training and better far transfer overall, with higher accuracy for digits than dots, especially among strong relational learners. Completing the digit task first selectively improved later transfer to the dots, which the authors suggest may reflect symbolic representations scaffolding relational alignment. The results indicate inference learning promotes abstract relational representations, with representational format and task order also shaping transfer.
papers.abstract: Abstraction of relational structures beyond surface features is essential for transfer of learning across contexts. However, learners often fail to apply relational knowledge outside the original learning setting. Our prior work shows that inference-learning can promote relational abstraction and supervised far transfer, but it remains unclear whether such learning supports spontaneous transfer without feedback. This study tested whether inference learning improves unsupervised far transfer across tasks with distinct surface characteristics. Participants learned to categorise stimuli based on monotonic versus non-monotonic relations among line lengths, under classification or inference-learning conditions. Transfer was assessed for luminance-based dot arrays and digit sequences, presented in counterbalanced order. Inference-learning led to stronger relational responding during training and significantly improved far transfer performance overall, even in the absence of feedback. Transfer accuracy was higher for digit sequences than dot arrays, particularly among participants who demonstrated strong relational learning. Moreover, an unexpected finding was that completing the digit task first selectively improved subsequent transfer to the dot task, suggesting that symbolic representations may scaffold relational alignment. These findings provide evidence that inference-learning fosters abstract relational representations that support far transfer, while also highlighting the role of representational format and task sequencing in enabling effective generalization.

papers.title: Decision as navigation
papers.authors: Sebastijan Veselic, Elena Gutierrez, Timothy Muller et al.
papers.summary: This review argues that when decisions require inferring or reusing relations between options, decision-relevant attributes may be assembled into a cognitive map in which options are locations in a metric space and choice resembles navigation. Such a representation could allow the brain to compute vector-like relations between options and reuse them across problems to support value comparison. By linking neuroeconomics with spatial navigation research, the framework offers testable predictions about how structured knowledge is organised and used for choice.
papers.abstract: Understanding choice requires explaining how the brain represents decision-relevant information and uses it to guide behaviour. Research on value-based decision-making has traditionally framed choice as assigning and comparing values, yielding significant insights into its neural basis. However, it has said less about how the structure of decision problems is represented and used during deliberation, particularly when relations between options must be inferred or reused across decision problems. Here, we review evidence suggesting that, in such choices, decision-relevant attributes are assembled into a cognitive map. In this map, options are represented as locations in a metric space, and choice can be framed as navigation. This may allow the brain to compute vector-like relations between options and reuse them across decision problems to support value comparison. By linking neuroeconomics and spatial navigation research, this framework generates testable predictions about how the brain organises and uses structured knowledge for choice.

papers.title: Echoes of Thought: Task Complexity, Inner Speech Analogs, and Prompt Design Shape LLMs' Response
papers.authors: Franziska Usée, Daniel Schad
papers.summary: Using the two-step task from the model-free/model-based reinforcement learning literature, the authors ran nine simulation studies varying task complexity and prompt design in GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs. GPT-3.5 showed model-based signatures in simplified task settings, lost them in de-simplified versions, and regained them with a prompt analogous to inner speech that required reflecting on past trials and anticipating future consequences. The open-weight models showed diminished model-based signatures under both de-simplified and facilitative conditions. The findings point to a role for structured reflective and anticipatory language in complex LLM behaviour, with similarities to and differences from human decision-making.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown impressive performance across a wide range of tasks, yet the mechanisms behind their response behavior remain poorly understood. Drawing on insights from cognitive science and the computational framework of model-free and model-based reinforcement learning (RL), we examined conditions under which GPT-3.5 and four open-weight LLMs can exhibit behavioral signatures of model-based RL in the two-step task, a well-established paradigm for studying human learning and decision-making. Across nine simulation studies, we varied the task complexity and prompt design to examine conditions under which previously reported model-based RL signatures could be replicated. We found that GPT-3.5 showed model-based RL signatures in simplified task settings, but that these effects disappeared under de-simplified task versions. Crucially, model-based reasoning signatures could be re-established when incorporating an inner speech-analog prompt, requiring the LLM agent to reflect on previous trials and anticipate consequences of future actions. For the open-weight LLMs tested, we observed diminished signatures of model-based reasoning under both de-simplified and facilitative task conditions. Our fine-grained analyses of behavioral learning dynamics highlight the role of structured reflective and anticipatory linguistic processes in enabling complex response patterns in LLMs and reveal both similarities to and differences from human decision-making patterns.

papers.title: Attention in model-based cognitive neuroscience: Mechanisms for optimization under constraint
papers.authors: Emily Ruth Weichart, Ryan Pierce Kirkpatrick, Jared Vance
papers.summary: This review organises the algorithms proposed to implement or give rise to "attention" in model-based cognitive neuroscience by function, across perception, decision-making and learning. It grounds each formalised process in the performance objectives it serves and the processing constraints that limit it. The aim is to address the vagueness of verbal theories while avoiding the conflation of similar-looking mechanisms that may not share a neural basis, giving a road map of computational-level solutions attributed to attention.
papers.abstract: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term ``attention’’ is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings. The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis. This review provides a function-first organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to ``attention'' at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning. We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them. In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that ``attention'' mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

papers.title: Memory precision fluctuates with theta rhythmicity in humans
papers.authors: Troy Houser, Riley Acker, Dagmar Zeithamova
papers.summary: Using a dense behavioural sampling approach, with an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase and varying delays before the to-be-remembered stimulus, the authors examined whether memory fluctuates rhythmically. Experiment 1 replicated the finding that associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with a best-fitting frequency of 8 Hz. Experiment 2 found that memory precision also fluctuates at theta rhythm, as predicted by hippocampal models with oscillating engagement of alternative processing pathways. The work suggests such fast fluctuations can be studied noninvasively and behaviourally in humans.
papers.abstract: Rodent research indicates that the hippocampus naturally oscillates between memory encoding and retrieval phases at theta rhythm, indicating that the timing of when information reaches the hippocampus can determine encoding success. However, non-invasively probing such oscillations is challenging in humans. Here, we employed a recently developed dense sampling approach to construct a time course of memory encoding success. Using an attention-grabbing cue expected to reset theta phase, we varied the delay between the cue and to-be-remembered stimulus. Experiment 1 replicated recent finding that human associative memory performance fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, with the best fitting frequency at 8 Hz. Experiment 2 tested and confirmed a new prediction that memory precision also fluctuates with theta rhythmicity, consistent with hippocampal models postulating oscillations in the relative engagement of alternative processing pathways. Together, these findings suggest that the rapid neural fluctuations underpinning memory processes are robust enough to be observed using the dense behavioral sampling approach. Moreover, this work substantiates models of episodic memory and provides new avenues to study models of hippocampal function in humas noninvasively, providing evidence from a purely behavioral approach that human mnemonic discrimination fluctuates with theta rhythm.

papers.title: Control Dilemmas Exist on Different Levels of Information Processing: Flexibility and Stability Trade off at the Task Level
papers.authors: Andrea Janker, Sebastian Musslick, Gesine Dreisbach
papers.summary: The authors proposed that a flexibility–stability trade-off may exist only within the same level of information processing, and tested this with a new paradigm in which participants switched between categorization tasks amid within-task or between-task distractors at the task level (Experiments 1–2) or the stimulus level (Experiment 3). Between-task distractors interfered less than within-task distractors at the task level, indicating shielding, but both interfered equally at the stimulus level, consistent with shielding being bypassed by automatic retrieval of learned stimulus-response associations. Across experiments, shielding on the previous trial improved performance on task repeats but impaired it on task switches, supporting a trade-off between stability and flexibility at the task level.
papers.abstract: Our cognitive system must manage two opposing demands: staying focused on one task (stability) and switching between tasks when needed (flexibility). Traditionally, a trade-off has been assumed between these two control modes. Recent studies questioned this idea. However, they do not consider that experimental manipulations can influence stability and flexibility at different levels of information processing and that a trade-off may only exist within the same level. We introduce a novel paradigm designed to investigate flexibility and stability at different levels of information processing (task vs. stimulus level). Participants switched between two categorization tasks while ignoring distractors. Distractors either came from the same (within-task) or the alternative task (between-task) and were either response-congruent or incongruent. In Experiments 1 and 2, participants categorized words superimposed on distractor images representing the generic response categories (task level interference). In Experiment 3, they categorized letters or digits flanked by distractor letters or digits (stimulus level interference). Reduced interference from between-task distractors compared to within-task distractors in Experiments 1 and 2 show shielding at the task level. At the stimulus level (Experiment 3) both distractor-types interfered to the same extent, indicating that the shielding against between-task distractors got bypassed by the automatic retrieval of learnt stimulus-response associations. Across all three experiments, shielding against between-task distractors in the previous trial improved subsequent performance, when the task repeated (i.e. it improved stability), but impaired performance, when the task switched (i.e. it impaired flexibility). This finding supports a trade-off between flexibility and stability at the task level.

papers.title: Morphological analysis when morphemes are hard to detect: evidence from infixation and reduplication
papers.authors: Dave Kenneth Tayao Cayado, Kathleen Rastle
papers.summary: Using the morpheme interference paradigm in Tagalog, the authors tested whether infixes (e.g., t-in-awag) and reduplicants (e.g., tatawag) are detected during prelexical processing, since these morphemes lack a consistent surface form. Nonwords with morphological structure produced lower accuracy and longer RTs than nonwords without, indicating that skilled readers are sensitive to these structures. This extends evidence for morphological analysis beyond English suffixation and bears on theories of morpheme learning.
papers.abstract: There is substantial psycholinguistic evidence that skilled reading involves morphological analysis, whereby morphologically complex words like teacher are recognised via constituent morphemes {teach}+{-er}. The ability to recognise morphemes is vital as it allows readers to interpret both familiar and unfamiliar words. However, over 50% of the evidence for this claim comes from studies of suffixation in English, where morphemes typically have a relatively consistent surface form across exemplars (clean in cleaner, cleanliness; -ed in walked, jumped). It remains unclear whether morphological analysis is also robust when morphemes lack a consistent surface form. Using the morpheme interference paradigm in Tagalog, we test whether infixes and reduplicants are detected during prelexical processing. Infixes are inserted within a stem and therefore reduce the consistency of its surface realisation (e.g., tawag → t-in-awag ‘called’), while reduplicants involve partial or full copying of a stem and therefore lack a consistent surface realisation (e.g., tawag and lundag become tatawag ‘will call’ and lulundag ‘will jump’, where ta- and lu- are instances of the same reduplicant morpheme). We found robust morpheme interference effects in both accuracy and RTs. Specifically, nonwords with morphological structure induced significantly lower accuracy and longer RTs than nonwords without. Our findings show skilled readers’ acquired sensitivity to these sophisticated morphological structures and motivate refinements to theories of morpheme learning.

papers.title: Retro-cue Characteristics and Visual Masking Differentially Influence Voluntary and Involuntary Attention
papers.authors: Germán A. Cipriani, Carlos González-García, Elisa Martín-Arévalo et al.
papers.summary: Across four experiments (n=140), the study manipulated retro-cue reliability and late visual masking with peripheral and central retro-cues, and analysed RTs and accuracy with hierarchical drift-diffusion models. Voluntary and involuntary retrospective attention did not differ in how they affected competing perceptual and semantic working memory content. Cue type, reliability and masking did influence voluntary and involuntary selection in other ways, for example masking altered involuntary benefits in opposite directions across representational quality and retrieval processes for peripheral cues.
papers.abstract: This study examined whether voluntary and involuntary retrospective attention prioritize competing working memory (WM) representations involving low-level perceptual features and high-level semantic categories. In external attention, interactions between attentional voluntariness and representational level have been reported, with voluntary and involuntary attention differentially modulating high- and low-level content. In contrast, previous WM studies using either central or peripheral retro-cues found no such interaction. We therefore tested whether increasing retro-cue predictivity and using fully non-predictive cues would reveal this dissociation. We also investigated whether late visual masking promotes retrospective attention by protecting WM representations from visual interference. Across four experiments (n=140), retro-cue reliability (Experiments 1a–1b) and late visual masking (Experiments 2a–2b) were manipulated using peripheral and central retro-cues. Reaction times and accuracy were modeled using hierarchical drift-diffusion modeling. Voluntariness did not differentially modulate competing perceptual and semantic WM contents. Furthermore, four novel findings emerged: (1) voluntary attentional benefits on WM representational quality were enabled by increasing the reliability of central retro-cues and operated through protection from visual interference; (2) reducing retro-cue predictivity from low to non-predictive had little effect on involuntary attention elicited by peripheral retro-cues, whereas evidence for central retro-cues remained ambiguous; (3) eliminating late visual masking generally did not reduce voluntary attentional deployment; and (4) for peripheral retro-cues, masking selectively altered involuntary attentional benefits across representational quality and retrieval processes in opposite directions, while increasing the difference between voluntary and involuntary attentional deployment. Together, these findings indicate that retro-cue type, reliability, and visual masking differentially influence voluntary and involuntary selection in WM without altering their relative effects on competing perceptual and semantic representations.

papers.title: Isolating domain-specific and domain-general contributions to global confidence
papers.authors: Sophie Bavard, Andrew McWilliams, Flora Chartier et al.
papers.summary: Using a gamified approach, the authors compared how global confidence, i.e. evaluation of performance over longer spans, is formed in memory versus perception. In memory, both local accuracy and local confidence contributed to global confidence, whereas in perception only local confidence predicted it. The results suggest that global confidence formation differs across cognitive domains, which is relevant to metacognitive interventions in education and psychiatry.
papers.abstract: While metacognition - our ability to evaluate our own cognitive processes - has been extensively studied by measuring trial-by-trial self-assessments of task performance (local confidence), real-world decisions often require a broader perspective, drawing on evaluations of performance over wider timespans (global confidence). Despite its pervasive influence on decision-making and mental health, it remains unknown whether global confidence is formed through similar or distinct processes across cognitive domains. Here we employ a novel gamified approach to compare how global confidence is formed in the domains of memory and perception. In memory, we found that both local accuracy and confidence contributed to global confidence, whereas in perception, global confidence was predicted by local confidence alone. By comparing the formation of global confidence across domains, our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underpinning self-evaluation, paving the way for the development of metacognitive interventions in education and psychiatry.

papers.title: Biased processing of multiple outcomes in human reinforcement learning: evidence from computational modeling and eye-tracking
papers.authors: Henri Vandendriessche, Gruson Charlotte, Antonios Nasioulas et al.
papers.summary: The authors designed a reinforcement learning task in which each choice yielded two outcomes from the same distribution, only one of which counted toward payoff, and combined behaviour, computational modelling and eye-tracking. Both outcomes influenced learning, but integration was biased toward rewards over punishments, and gaze was modulated by outcome valence and relevance. A second experiment with complete feedback confirmed the main results, suggesting that losses tend to be neglected relative to gains when multiple outcomes are delivered.
papers.abstract: In many circumstances, choices result in multiple simultaneous outcomes, all of which should be integrated to optimally update reward expectation. Yet, to date, empirical investigations of reinforcement learning have mostly focused on situations where choices deliver only one outcome at a time. To understand how humans learn from multiple outcomes, we designed a new reinforcement learning task, where the selection of an option resulted in two outcomes drawn from the same underlying distribution over potential gains and losses, even if ultimately only one of the two counted for the final payoff. Behavioral results show that the two - equally informative- outcomes are considered, yet asymmetrically as function of their valence. This behavioral observation is backed up by computational analyses showing that, on top of previously documented asymmetric update, multiple outcome integration is biased, such as it overweighs rewards over punishments. Behavioral and computational results were paralleled by eye-tracking analysis showing that attention deployment is biased by outcome valence and relevance. The main results were confirmed in a second experiment featuring complete feedback information. Overall, our findings suggest that, when options deliver multiple discordant outcomes, losses tend to be neglected compared to gains.

papers.title: Learning to Enumerate Reorganizes Magnitude Representations
papers.authors: Lauren S Aulet
papers.summary: The authors trained ResNeXt-50 networks to enumerate dots and linearly decoded number versus cumulative area from penultimate-layer features. Untrained networks showed an area bias, whereas enumeration training reversed it within one epoch by suppressing area information, an effect not mirrored by a control network trained on area. This is a computational proof of concept that learning to enumerate can reorganise magnitude representations, suggesting the adult number bias may partly follow from symbolic number acquisition.
