papers.abstract: Human adults show a number bias in magnitude perception, weighting numerical information more heavily than continuous magnitudes like area. However, developmental research suggests this bias is not innate: young children show an area bias that reverses to a number bias only later in development. What drives this shift? Here we use deep neural networks as a tool for testing computational sufficiency, asking whether learning to estimate number is by itself enough to reorganize how a visual system weights magnitude. We trained ResNeXt-50 networks on an enumeration task (labeling the number of dots in an image, an operationalization of a functional outcome of counting) and measured representational bias by linearly decoding number versus cumulative area from penultimate-layer features, with the two dimensions decorrelated by design. Untrained networks showed a robust area bias, with area more decodable than number. Critically, networks trained to estimate number showed a reversal, with number becoming substantially more decodable than area, and this shift emerged after a single epoch of training. The effect was not a trivial consequence of training on a dimension: a matched control trained to estimate area did not produce the mirror-image effect, because enumeration training actively suppressed area information rather than merely amplifying number. Principal component analysis confirmed a reorganization of representational geometry, with numerosity becoming the dominant axis of variation (r² = 0.95) and area variance strongly reduced. These findings provide a computational proof-of-concept that learning to enumerate can restructure magnitude representations, suggesting that the perceptual primacy of number in adults may be partly a consequence, rather than a precondition, of symbolic number acquisition.

papers.title: The Not So Illusory Truth Effect: Source Credibility and the Effect of Repetition on Belief
papers.authors: Reed Orchinik, David Gertler Rand, Rahul Bhui
papers.summary: The authors present a formal model arguing that the illusory truth effect can be rational when sources are usually truthful, and which predicts little repetition effect for non-credible sources. In a preregistered experiment (N = 4,947) the effect was substantially smaller in a mostly false than a mostly true newsfeed, and in a second (N = 2,484) repetition raised partisans' belief only for claims from the 2024 U.S. presidential candidate they trusted. Repeated misinformation may therefore be most persuasive when it comes from trusted sources.
papers.abstract: The illusory truth effect, in which repetition increases belief, is often seen as a cognitive bias. Here, we argue that it may reflect a rational adaptation to generally high-quality information environments. A formal model shows that increasing belief in repeated statements improves accuracy when a source usually tells the truth but sometimes errs. The model captures previous findings and, unlike existing accounts, predicts that repetition should do little to increase belief when the source is not credible. In a large (N = 4,947) preregistered experiment with a quota-matched U.S. sample, the effect was substantially smaller when headlines appeared in a mostly false rather than mostly true newsfeed. In a second preregistered experiment (N = 2,484), repetition increased partisans' belief only in claims from the 2024 U.S. presidential candidate they trusted. Repeated misinformation may therefore be most persuasive when it comes from sources people trust.

papers.title: When “they” is singular: The interplay between cognitive and social factors predicts pronoun misinterpretations in bilingual English speakers
papers.authors: Manuel F. Pulido, Stanislav Mulík, Paola E. Dussias
papers.summary: Using self-paced reading, the study examined processing of non-binary singular 'they' in unambiguous and temporarily ambiguous contexts among second-language English speakers from Spain. Seemingly chance-level group performance reflected bimodal distributions of interpretation, with misinterpretations predicted by combined sociodemographic and cognitive factors, and even participants willing to adopt non-binary language depended on cognitive resources for accurate interpretation. The authors use these findings to propose a conceptual model of adaptation to grammatical change, termed IMAGINE.
papers.abstract: Language change is shaped by cognitive biases as well as by sociolinguistic perceptions of linguistic innovation. Although the use of they as a singular pronoun to refer to a generic referent is not new in English (e.g., "An employee can file a complaint if they need to"), a recent innovation extends this usage to refer to known individuals of non-binary gender. This type of socially motivated language change allows speakers to position themselves relative to linguistic innovation. Using the self-paced reading paradigm, we examined the processing of non-binary singular they across unambiguous (one-referent) and temporarily ambiguous (two-referent) contexts. We report on a processing experiment with second-language English speakers from Spain who, by virtue of their bilingual experience, are skilled at language learning and regulating activation of competing representations through cognitive control. We investigate how variability in the adoption of the pronominal innovation is influenced by sociodemographic and cognitive factors. We find that seemingly at-chance group-level performance in resolving temporary ambiguities is the product of bimodal distributions in interpretation within the population. Lingering misinterpretations in some speakers are predicted by a combination of sociodemographic and cognitive factors. Critically, we find that even among participants willing to adopt non-binary language, accurate interpretation of the non-binary singular they is mediated by cognitive resources. The findings bear implications for accounts of language change and the adoption of non-binary pronouns in bilingual communities as a result of individual variability. We outline a proposal for a conceptual Integrated Model of Adaptation to Grammar In Evolution ("IMAGINE").

papers.title: Flexibility of hierarchical reasoning across age and species
papers.authors: Abhishek M. Dedhe, Stephen Ferrigno, Diana A. Liao et al.
papers.summary: Using Bayesian modelling of previously published and new data from US adults, Tsimane adults, 3-to-6-year-old children, rhesus monkeys and carrion crows, the study tested hierarchical reasoning across task complexities and stimulus domains. Evidence for hierarchical reasoning appeared across ages and species, with substantial individual and population variation; adults relied on it most consistently, while children and non-humans showed graded performance depending on complexity and stimulus type. The authors conclude that hierarchical reasoning is a flexible, not all-or-none, ability that may not be uniquely human.
papers.abstract: Hierarchical reasoning underlies complex abilities such as language, mathematics, and tool-use. In this study, we examined how hierarchical reasoning flexibly varies in adults across cultures, children, crows, and monkeys. We also tested hierarchical reasoning across varied task complexities and with stimuli from both visual-perceptual and semantic-conceptual relational domains. We conducted Bayesian modelling analyses with both previously published data (Ferrigno et al., 2020; Liao et al., 2022) and newly collected data. These data were cumulatively from US adults, Tsimane adults from an indigenous community at a field location in Bolivia, 3-to-6-year-old US children, rhesus monkeys, and carrion crows. We found evidence for hierarchical reasoning across age and species, though with much individual and cross-population variation. Adults exhibited the most consistent reliance on hierarchical mechanisms, while children and non-humans showed graded performance influenced by task complexity and stimulus type. In summary, the deployment of hierarchical mechanisms varies across contexts rather than operating as an all-or-none capability. These findings suggest that hierarchical reasoning may be a flexible ability-not necessarily unique to humans, but rather emerging through incremental increases in cognitive capacities across development and evolution.

papers.title: Time after time: neural codes of speech comprehension
papers.authors: Laura Gwilliams
papers.summary: This review argues that the brain converts the transient speech signal into neural representations that are persistent, parallel and time-stamped. It covers evidence for persistence of information after it leaves the acoustic input, parallel encoding of recent inputs across levels of linguistic structure, and dynamic codes representing both content and elapsed time to preserve order. Together these properties are proposed to explain how a vanishing signal yields temporally extended linguistic structure.
papers.abstract: The acoustic signal of speech is fleeting and unfolds linearly; yet listeners must derive temporally extended and hierarchically organized linguistic structures to comprehend it. This article reviews evidence that the human brain transforms the transient auditory signal into neural representations that are persistent, parallel, and time-stamped. First, neural persistence allows information to remain available after it has disappeared from the acoustic input. Second, parallel encoding of recent inputs across multiple levels of language structure enables composition and interactions across the speech hierarchy. Third, dynamic neural representations encode both content and elapsed time, providing a flexible mechanism for preserving sequence order. Together, these representational properties reveal how the human brain transforms a continuously disappearing signal into temporally extended linguistic structures.

papers.title: Task-dependent inflation of rapid motion priming effects due to task and response constraints
papers.authors: Kimberley Dundas, Mary A. Peterson, Joseph L. Brooks
papers.summary: Across two experiments, the authors tested whether visual motion priming estimates from tasks requiring individuated perception of two briefly presented stimuli (e.g., same-different judgements) are inflated at very short durations and ISIs. At the shortest timings observers were at chance discriminating the prime's direction and often reported seeing only one stimulus, suggesting responses driven by task demands; tasks not requiring explicit discrimination still showed priming but with substantially smaller magnitude. The authors recommend paradigms that minimise such task-related biases.
papers.abstract: Visual motion priming (VMP) arises when an unambiguous stimulus clearly moving in one direction (e.g., leftwards) induces the perception that a subsequent ambiguous motion stimulus is moving in the same direction. VMP can be observed with very brief stimulus presentations and inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs) of only tens of milliseconds. Anecdotal evidence suggests that, under such conditions, observers may be unable to reliably individuate the prime and ambiguous stimuli. We argue that, for VMP measurement tasks which rely on individuated perception of the motion direction of the two stimuli (e.g., same-different comparisons), this limitation may inflate estimates of VMP. Across two experiments, we observed priming effects with such tasks. However, at the shortest presentation durations and ISIs, observers were at chance for discriminating the motion direction of the initial priming stimulus and frequently reported perceiving only one stimulus. We argue that, under these conditions, participants may rely on task demands rather than distinct percepts to make responses, biasing them to report the same motion direction for both stimuli which is interpreted as VMP. Consistent with this account, analysis of data from alternative tasks that do not require explicit discrimination of the two stimuli still showed VMP, but with substantially reduced magnitude. These findings suggest that VMP magnitude estimates can be inflated by response procedures that depend on conscious discrimination of briefly presented motion stimuli separated by very short intervals. We therefore recommend using paradigms that minimise such task-related biases when estimating VMP under these conditions.

papers.title: Stage-specific contributions of dorsal and ventral premotor cortices to the acquisition of arbitrary visuomotor associations
papers.authors: Sonia Turrini, Anastasia Amadori, Giorgio Arcara et al.
papers.summary: In 19 healthy adults, cTBS was applied to PMd, PMv or a V1 control before learning arbitrary visuomotor mappings, with a 24-hour recall test and state-space and Rescorla-Wagner modelling. Disrupting either PMd or PMv slowed early acquisition similarly, but only PMd disruption impaired next-day recall, which then depended on sleep quality and was decoupled from learning-day performance. The results indicate a stage-specific dissociation, with both regions supporting early learning and only PMd supporting stabilisation.
papers.abstract: The acquisition and consolidation of arbitrary visuomotor mappings (AVMMs) engage premotor regions, yet the distinct contributions of the dorsal (PMd) and ventral (PMv) premotor cortices remain unclear. Here, we applied continuous theta-burst stimulation (cTBS) immediately before AVMM learning to transiently disrupt PMd, PMv, or an occipital control site (V1) in 19 healthy young adults, using a within-subjects design. Participants learned arbitrary stimulus–response associations through trial-and-error feedback and completed a 24-hour delayed recall test. Trial-by-trial accuracy and reaction times were modeled using state-space and Rescorla–Wagner frameworks to quantify learning dynamics, prediction errors, and stabilization across days. Disruption of both PMd and PMv slowed early acquisition of AVMMs to a comparable extent relative to V1. However, only PMd disruption additionally impaired next-day recall, rendering recall performance dependent on sleep quality and decoupled from learning-day performance, whereas recall following PMv disruption remained comparable to the control condition. These findings indicate that PMd, but not PMv, contributes to the stabilization of newly learned visuomotor associations, providing causal, stage-specific evidence for a functional dissociation within the human premotor cortex: PMv and PMd support early rule formation and exploratory learning, whereas only PMd contributes to subsequent stabilization of newly learned visuomotor associations. Furthermore, they emphasize the modulatory influence of sleep on memory retention when consolidation processes are compromised, advancing mechanistic models of premotor contributions to associative sensorimotor learning.

papers.title: Leveraging word knowledge from everyday language
papers.authors: Layla Unger, Emma James
papers.summary: The authors quantified contextual cues in children's everyday English language input, based on the idea that words with similar meanings occur in similar contexts, as exploited by large language models. These context cues reliably predicted real-world word learning beyond other established predictors. The findings suggest that everyday language context helps scaffold children's vocabulary acquisition.
papers.abstract: Within the first few years of life, children go from nonverbal infants to fluent users of hundreds of words. This feat unfolds as children are immersed in a sea of words in conversations, stories, and other language contexts. In principle, word contexts might support word learning because words with similar meanings tend to occur in similar contexts. Thus, a child who knows some fruit words and has heard them in the context of "juicy" might learn that a "juicy mango" is also a fruit even without ever seeing a mango. Indeed, cutting-edge large language models leverage just these context cues to form rich representations of words. Yet we do not know whether these cues are an important driver of real-world word learning. We quantified context cues in children's everyday English language input and found that they did reliably predict real-world word learning, above and beyond other established predictors. These findings illuminate how everyday language scaffolds word learning.

papers.title: Why are pictures remembered better than sounds? The roles of subjective vividness of mental imagery and semantic labels
papers.authors: F. N. Ahmad, S. Tremblay, M. Alvi et al.
papers.summary: Across experiments, participants generated a mental image from a written label and rated its vividness before an old/new recognition judgement for pictures or environmental sounds. Pictures showed higher vividness and recognition than sounds; written labels raised vividness and target recognition for sounds and eliminated modality differences for targets, but pictures retained an advantage in lure discrimination. Vividness predicted correct target recognition for pictures but also increased false recognition of lures for sounds, suggesting the picture advantage for lures reflects stronger item-specific retrieval information.
papers.abstract: Pictures are recognized more accurately than environmental sounds, possibly because pictures provide enhanced conceptual and perceptual representations than sounds. Conceptual-perceptual distinctiveness (CPD) theory proposes that pictures benefit from stronger semantic organization and more diagnostic perceptual detail. It remains unclear whether the picture superiority effect reflects differences in the subjective vividness of retrieved memories and whether increasing category-level semantic support can enhance vividness for environmental sounds, thereby reducing picture superiority in recognition memory. Vividness was assessed independently of recognition by having participants generate a mental image from a written label and rate its vividness before old/new judgment of the recognition probe. Experiment 1 replicated the picture superiority effect, with pictures producing higher vividness and recognition accuracy than sounds. In Experiments 2A and 2B, written labels strengthened category-level semantic support for sounds, increasing vividness and target recognition and eliminating modality differences for targets. However, pictures continued to show superior lure (i.e., exemplar foil) discrimination and higher vividness preceding accurate lure rejection. Generalized linear mixed-effects (GLMM) analyses showed that vividness selectively predicted correct target recognition for pictures, whereas for sounds, greater vividness also increased false recognition of lures. Together, these findings suggest that semantic support enhances vividness of mental imagery and target recognition for sounds, whereas the picture superiority effect for lure recognition reflects stronger item-specific retrieval information.

papers.title: A match made in mental space: Alignment between target skew and cue organization influences recall of attribute values
papers.authors: Patrik Sörqvist, Emil Skog, Alice Mason et al.
papers.summary: The authors propose that retrieval cues, like targets, are organised by distinctiveness and that recall is best when cue and target distributions align. In a preregistered experiment using old (skewed) and new (more linear) EU energy-label scales as cues for recalling refrigerators' kWh values drawn from skewed or non-skewed distributions, the linear scale produced more accurate recall for non-skewed targets but overly linear recall for skewed targets. The skewed scale worked best when targets were positively skewed, indicating that cues impose distributional structure on reconstructed values.
papers.abstract: Recall is often more successful for items from sparse (distinct) regions and less successful from dense (less distinct) regions in memory space. We propose that retrieval cues are also organized into crowded and less crowded regions depending on distinctiveness, and that successful retrieval depends on the distributional match between the organization of targets and cues. As a real-world test case, we used the labels from the European Union's old (A+++, A++, A+, A, B, C, D) and new (A, B, C, D, E, F, G) energy-label scale as cues for memory retrieval of appliances' kilowatt-hour (kWh) values. In a preregistered experiment, participants rated seven refrigerators, while studying associated kWh values drawn from a positive, a negative, or a non-skewed distribution. Ratings confirmed that the labels of the old scale were psychologically skewed in mental space whereas the new scale had a more linear organization. After a brief filled delay, labels served as retrieval cues for kWh recall. Analyses of recall patterns, complemented by analyses of recall error, showed that the linear cue scale yielded recalled values that were closer to the correct kWh values when target values were non-skewed, but recalled values were overly linear when targets were skewed. Conversely, recall was most successful with the skewed cue scale when target values were positively skewed. These findings suggest that retrieval cues constrain reconstruction by imposing a distributional structure on target representations, and that recall is most successful when this structure aligns with the organization of encoded values in mental space.

papers.title: Factors Influencing the Emergence of Dependency Length Minimization in Neural Agent Simulations
papers.authors: Yuqing Zhang, Tessa Verhoef, Gertjan van Noord et al.
papers.summary: Using a framework in which recurrent neural network agents learn and communicate in artificial languages, the study examined how listening noise, limited speaker capacity and incremental processing affect the emergence of dependency length minimization. Results showed a complex interplay: agents regularised toward one dominant order in the full meaning space, showed a short-before-long preference aligned with DLM only in verb-initial languages in the half meaning space, and showed a consistent DLM preference only under incremental processing pressure. This suggests processing limitations may shape DLM, while highlighting the difficulty of modelling human-like biases in emergent communication.
papers.abstract: Given various grammatical options, language users prefer the word order choice that reduces the overall length of syntactic dependencies, a principle known as dependency length minimization (DLM). The origins of this preference remain an open question, particularly whether it originates from constraints on efficient information processing. Computational simulations provide a powerful approach to identifying the factors influencing the emergence of linguistic phenomena. However, previous simulations of DLM have not examined realistic interaction contexts and have produced mixed results. The present study investigates the emergence of DLM in artificial languages using a recently proposed language learning and communication framework based on recurrent neural networks. In this framework, agents are trained to speak and interpret artificial languages and then use these languages to communicate. Using this framework, we study the impact of several factors related to processing limitations in a communicative setting, such as noise during listening, limited speaker capacity, and incremental sentence processing. Our results reveal a complex interplay among these factors in shaping word order preferences in neural agents. Specifically, in the full meaning space, agents regularize toward a single dominant word order, while in the half meaning space, they show a short-before-long preference that only aligns with DLM in verb-initial languages. A consistent DLM preference emerges only when agents are subject to incremental processing pressure. These results suggest that limitations in human cognitive processing may indeed play a role in shaping DLM. Our findings provide insights into the conditions under which neural models replicate human-like preferences for minimizing syntactic dependency distances and highlight the challenges of designing emergent communication models that capture human cognitive biases in language processing.

papers.title: More Evidence for the Standard Account of Theory of Mind Development: A Reply to Fabricius (2026)
papers.authors: Hannes Rakoczy, Lydia Schidelko
papers.summary: This is a reply to Fabricius, who argued that the authors' earlier results support a competence-limitation account in which children lack proper mental state concepts until about age 6–7. The authors argue that their original findings are incompatible with that account. They say the findings fit the standard picture, in which children acquire mental state concepts by age 4 and performance factors sometimes mask this competence.
papers.abstract: Fabricius argues that the results of a recent study of ours speak for a deflationary competence limitation account of Theory of Mind development. According to this account, children do not operate with proper mental state concepts until age 6-7 or older. However, the original findings are, in fact, incompatible with such competence limitation accounts, but compatible with the standard picture of Theory of Mind development: According to this picture, children acquire proper mental state concepts by age 4, but this competence is sometimes masked by performance factors.

papers.title: Perception of visual noise patterns depends on correlations produced in V1: A simulation study
papers.authors: Shaozhi Nie, Samantha A. Montoya, Michael-Paul Schallmo et al.
papers.summary: Using the biologically inspired VOneNet model of V1, the authors simulated responses to visual noise and analyzed single-unit responses and correlations among model neurons. Spatially independent noise still produced population correlations, and decorrelating the simulated activity substantially degraded reconstruction of the noise pattern, with simple-cell correlations contributing most. The authors conclude that noise perception depends on population-level correlations in V1 and discuss implications for visual snow syndrome.
papers.abstract: Visual noise is widely used as a stimulus in vision science, yet the neural representation of noise itself remains poorly understood. We investigated how external visual noise is encoded in the primary visual cortex (V1) using a biologically inspired neural network model (VOneNet). We simulated V1 responses to noise patterns and analyzed both the response of individual model neurons and the correlations among them. As expected, simulated neurons with smaller receptive fields showed stronger responses. Importantly, spatially independent noise stimuli elicited correlations across the population. These correlations were critical for reconstructing the original noise pattern in a reconstruction analysis that served as a probe of perceptual representation: decorrelating modeled neural activity substantially degraded reconstruction quality. Correlations among simulated simple cells, rather than complex cells, played a dominant role in encoding external noise. Our findings suggest that the perception of visual noise depends not only on local neural activity but also on population-level correlations in V1. Implications for visual snow syndrome, a condition in which illusory external noise is perceived, are discussed.

papers.title: Ocularity modulates the dominance of spatial over temporal influences in binocular rivalry
papers.authors: Lisa Beckmann, Thomas Schenk, Karin Ludwig
papers.summary: The study examined how spatial context (surround inhibition) and temporal context (flash suppression) combine in binocular rivalry, manipulating their strengths by varying which eye received the prime, surround, and center stimuli. When both influences biased perception in the same direction they were mostly additive, and some combinations allowed near-perfect prediction of the dominant percept. When they conflicted, spatial context generally dominated, except when both were presented interocularly, where temporal context had the edge. The authors attribute this to flash suppression being weakened less by interocular presentation than surround inhibition, suggesting different hierarchical processing levels.
papers.abstract: The perception of a binocular rivalry (BR) stimulus can be influenced by other stimuli in temporal or spatial proximity. Here, we investigate how spatial (surround inhibition [SI]) and temporal context (flash suppression [FS]) interact. Previously, we modulated these influences by varying surround contrast in SI and timing parameters in FS. In the present study, we make use of the fact that the strengths of the two contexts can also be manipulated in the same way, namely by modulating ocularity. We varied FS strength by showing the prime to the same eye as the identical probe or to the other eye. Spatial influence was varied by presenting the surround to the same eye as the matching center, to the other eye, or to both. Temporal and spatial influences were mostly additive when biasing perception in the same direction. Some combinations were so strong that the dominant percept could be predicted almost perfectly. This may help in deliberately creating desired perceptual outcomes in future studies. Spatial context tended to dominate in conflicting situations. When both context types were presented interocularly (and presumably weaker), however, temporal context had the edge. This may reflect the unexpectedly strong interocular FS: the interocular constellation weakened FS much less than SI, suggesting differences in hierarchical processing levels. Thus, comparing interocular conditions may have been less informative than anticipated. Still, when the conflicting influences were both working intraocularly, spatial context dominated, consistent with previous findings.

papers.title: The Precision Hierarchy Hypothesis: A Unifying Framework to Explain Opposing Serial Effects
papers.authors: Carina Ufer, Helen Blank
papers.summary: This theoretical paper proposes the "precision hierarchy hypothesis" to reconcile attractive and repulsive serial dependence effects. Within a predictive processing framework, it holds that highly precise priors at lower sensory levels yield repulsive effects, while lower-precision priors at higher, more abstract levels yield attractive biases, with prior precision adjusting to environmental correlations. The authors say the framework unifies diverse findings and offers testable predictions.
papers.abstract: Serial dependence, the phenomenon where current perception is biased toward the previous stimulus, has been interpreted as a mechanism for perceptual stability, smoothing variability in sensory input. However, analyses that include both the previous stimulus and previous response unmasked repulsive effects at the sensory level that were otherwise concealed. Moreover, attractive serial biases fail to scale with environmental correlations, challenging their primary role in maintaining stability. We propose the "precision hierarchy hypothesis," grounded in predictive processing, as a unifying framework for these seemingly contradictory findings. Repulsive effects naturally emerge when priors-shaped by recent trials-are highly precise, making small deviations in incoming input more probable under alternative priors. We further propose that prior precision decreases across hierarchical levels. A higher precision at lower sensory levels leads to repulsive effects, as even small deviations in incoming signal are in conflict with the prior. In contrast, attractive biases emerge at higher, more abstract levels, where deviations are integrated with broader conceptual priors. By dynamically shaping prior precision according to environmental correlations, perception remains adaptive, balancing the need for stability with the sensitivity to detect meaningful changes in the environment. This framework reconciles diverse findings on serial effects and provides testable predictions for future research.

papers.title: Do Generative Priors Align with Human Naturalness Perception?
papers.authors: Taiki Fukiage
papers.summary: The authors probed the native prediction errors of 25 image and video generative models using content-preserving interventions that disrupt facial configuration or physical illumination consistency. Loss differences reproduced the Thatcher effect and shape-dependent responses to illumination inconsistencies, tracked graded human naturalness judgments (up to r = .84 for faces and .64 for physical scenes), and retained human-aligned signal after controlling for vision-encoder feature distances and image quality metrics. Alignment with humans peaked earlier along denoising schedules than sensitivity did, suggesting that human-like naturalness judgments dissociate from generic violation detection.
papers.abstract: Visual generative models are trained to capture the probability distributions of natural images, yet whether their native priors reflect the regularities governing human perception of image naturalness remains an open question. Here, we probe these priors through native prediction errors across 25 open image and video generators. Because raw single-image losses are dominated by scene content and visual complexity, we evaluate directional loss differences using content-preserving, paired relational interventions that selectively disrupt facial configurations or physical illumination consistency while limiting changes in low-level image statistics. Across both domains, these loss differences reproduce human-like selective sensitivities and tolerances, capturing the classic Thatcher effect on faces and shape-dependent responses to illumination inconsistencies. Notably, these loss differences reliably track continuous gradations of human naturalness judgments across individual stimulus pairs (peaking at $r = .84$ on faces and $.64$ on physical scenes) and retain unique human-aligned signals even after controlling for feature distances from frozen vision encoders and standard image quality metrics. We also find that while overall sensitivity to these violations broadly covaries with human alignment across models, the two systematically decouple along denoising schedules, with alignment peaking earlier than sensitivity, revealing that human-like naturalness judgments dissociate from generic violation detection. Together, these findings demonstrate that learning visual distributions yields generative loss landscapes that capture distinct aspects of human naturalness perception.

papers.title: Examining Social Attribution in LLM Reasoning: A Theory-Guided Probing Methodology
papers.authors: Zhaoxin Yu, Qingchao Kong, Dajun Zeng et al.
papers.summary: The paper builds a benchmark of 7,639 responsibility and blame judgment questions, drawn from classic Attribution Theory vignettes and real-world narratives, and evaluates 32 LLMs and 5 non-LLM baselines. It also uses probing to examine how five attribution dimensions are represented in hidden states. LLMs showed measurable but incomplete agreement with human judgments, which increased with model size. Some attribution dimensions were decodable from particular hidden-state positions, and their influence on judgments was consistent with Attribution Theory.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in sociotechnical systems where social attribution, the reasoning process attributing external events to the causes and reasons of agents' social behaviors, plays a critical role. These processes involve judgments of social cause, responsibility, and blame/credit to agents. Although attributional models are well-studied in social psychology and cognition through Attribution Theory, social attribution remains underexplored in AI, particularly LLM social reasoning. This paper provides the first systematic exploration of LLM social attribution. Our work focuses on responsibility and blame attributions, examining current LLMs' judgments and their underlying internal mechanisms. Guided by attribution theory, we construct a social attribution benchmark consisting of a Vignette subset based on classic scenarios from attribution theory research and a Reality subset based on real-world social narratives, yielding 7,639 responsibility/blame judgment questions. On this basis, we evaluate 32 representative LLMs and 5 basic non-LLM baselines. To further explore the internal mechanisms underlying the LLM judgment process, we develop a probing-based methodology to investigate the latent-space representations of 5 key attribution dimensions and the consistency of their influences on LLM judgments compared to those in human social attribution. Our research findings reveal that current LLMs exhibit measurable but incomplete agreement with human responsibility and blame judgments, and meanwhile, this agreement is positively correlated with model size. Some attribution dimensions are systematically decodable from specific positions in LLM hidden states, and their influences on the final judgment are consistent with those indicated by human Attribution Theory. The dataset and associated code are available at https://github.com/Yuzhaoxin946/SAB-Bench.

papers.title: The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Obada Kraishan
papers.summary: The study tested whether longer reasoning reduces cognitive biases in LLMs, using 30 vignettes across six biases, four model families with reasoning and non-reasoning siblings, and four thinking-token ceilings (12,350 API calls). Reasoning models were not reliably less biased than their siblings, and bias did not reliably decline with more realized reasoning tokens. Only anchoring went in the human direction (d = 1.89), while most other biases leaned the opposite way. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor lowered anchoring on all five items but did not reach significance (p = .057). The authors argue against treating test-time reasoning as a guarantee of rationality.
papers.abstract: Reasoning models allocate extra computation at inference time and present their answers as the product of deliberate thought. If this deliberation works the way dual-process accounts of human cognition suggest, longer thinking should weaken the classic decision biases that fast, intuitive judgment produces. Using 30 vignettes covering six biases (anchoring, framing, loss aversion, escalation of commitment, availability, confirmation) from an established benchmark, we run a dose-response study across four model families, pairing each reasoning model with a matched non-reasoning sibling and requesting thinking ceilings of 0, 1,024, 4,096, and 8,192 tokens, for 12,350 API calls. Because a requested ceiling is not the same as realized deliberation, we use the reasoning tokens each call consumed as the dose. First, reasoning models are not less biased than their siblings; the point estimate leans the other way in every family, but the item-level pooled contrast is not reliable (Delta = +0.031, t(29) = 1.45, p = .157). Second, bias magnitude does not reliably fall as realized deliberation grows: no slope is significantly negative, and where anything moves it is the signed score drifting further from the human direction. Third, anchoring is the only bias in the human direction (d = 1.89). Four of the other five lean the opposite way in all seven models; with five items per bias, that reversal is reliable for framing and directional for escalation of commitment, confirmation, and loss aversion, while availability is absent. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor before answering lowered anchoring on all five anchoring items, which no amount of additional thinking did, although the effect does not reach significance (p = .057). The results argue against treating test-time reasoning as a rationality guarantee and for auditing deployed models bias by bias.

papers.title: Illusory Pattern Perception Drives Spurious Inference in Large Language Models
papers.authors: Peihua Mai, Zhuoyan Shao, Xinbao Qiao et al.
papers.summary: The paper adapts classic psychological paradigms to three tasks to study illusory pattern perception in LLMs, comparing them directly with human behavior. LLMs often showed stronger illusory pattern perception than humans, such as over-associating frequent positive attributes with majority groups or large organizations and building causal narratives from ambiguous events. A Sparse Autoencoder-based interpretability analysis linked holistic frequency perception and analytic cognitive orientation to these illusions, suggesting a threat to the reliability of LLM reasoning.

papers.title: Familiar Content Changes Performance and Processing in Matrix Reasoning in Early Adolescence
papers.authors: Paulo Guirro Laurence, Marcela M. Weiss, Elizeu Macedo
papers.summary: In a within-participants study of 56 Brazilian children and adolescents aged 11–15, accuracy and gaze patterns were compared on six abstract and six contextual 3×3 matrix-reasoning items requiring corresponding rules. Contextual items were answered more accurately (2.44 times higher odds of a correct response), while completion time, fixation count, and fixation duration were similar. Clustering of gaze transitions found two patterns, and contextual items were less likely to show the localized pattern. Broader exploration was linked to higher accuracy only for abstract items. These exploratory findings suggest abstract and familiar items are not interchangeable.
papers.abstract: Matrix-reasoning assessments commonly use abstract geometric figures, although familiar content may change both performance and processing. This within-participants study compared accuracy and gaze-defined patterns of visual exploration for abstract and contextual items requiring corresponding relational rules. Participants were 56 children and adolescents recruited from a public school in São Paulo, Brazil, aged 11 to 15 years. Each participant completed six abstract and six contextual 3 × 3 matrices while gaze was recorded. Trial-level transition matrices were constructed from fixation sequences across nine matrix cells and the response alternatives, and k-means clustering identified two recurring patterns. Contextual items were answered more accurately than abstract items, with 2.44 times higher odds of a correct response. Completion time, fixation count, and fixation duration were similar between conditions. Cluster 1 was characterized by localized transitions involving the final row and response alternatives, whereas Cluster 2 involved broader, more sequential exploration across the matrix. Contextual items had lower odds of Cluster 1 classification, indicating that representational format modestly altered the distribution of gaze patterns. A significant condition-by-cluster interaction further showed that Cluster 2 was associated with higher accuracy for abstract items, but no cluster difference was detected for contextual items. These exploratory findings suggest that familiar content changes how matrices are explored, indicating that abstract and familiar matrix items should not be treated as interchangeable.

papers.title: Breaking Common Ground through Reciprocal Misalignment
papers.authors: Siham Abu Ali, Tatiana Philippova, Isaac Fradkin
papers.summary: Four experiments used a multiplayer word association task with human or simulated partners who varied in semantic typicality, to test whether interaction inherently leads to semantic alignment. In general, social interaction led people to produce more conventional associations, but with an atypical or hard-to-align partner they reduced their own typicality and matching, sacrificing alignment even when incentivized to align. The authors interpret this "reciprocal misalignment" as possibly reflecting socially motivated differentiation rather than only coordination failure.
papers.abstract: Establishing shared meaning is widely considered the normative, almost ubiquitous trajectory of linguistic interaction, while moments of misalignment are typically viewed as temporary interruptions that individuals attempt to repair. However, it is not uncommon to experience communication breakdowns that actively escalate rather than resolve. This raises a fundamental question: does interaction inherently lead people toward shared meaning, or is semantic alignment a reciprocal, socially contingent process? We conducted four experiments using a novel multiplayer word association task, where participants generated semantic associations while interacting with either human or simulated partners varying in semantic typicality. Our results show that, in general, social interaction motivates individuals to produce more conventional associations to support alignment. However, this tendency depended on partner’s behavior: when interacting with an atypical or difficult-to-align-with partner, individuals actively reduced their own typicality and tendency to match partner’s associations, effectively sacrificing semantic alignment. Such ‘reciprocal misalignment’ persisted even when participants were incentivized to maximize alignment. Our findings suggest that semantic misalignment may reflect a reciprocal, socially-motivated modulation of identity and differentiation, rather than solely a failure of coordination. This work sheds light on the interactional mechanisms underlying interpersonal distancing, communication breakdowns in neurodivergence, and potentially broader patterns of social polarization.

papers.title: Selective maintenance of aversive memories as a mechanism of spontaneous recovery of fear
papers.summary: The authors fit computational models of a new theory, selective maintenance of aversive memories, to fear conditioning and extinction behavior (N=316), and found they captured spontaneous recovery and outperformed alternative theory-based models. Results held in a preregistered replication (N=355) and a symptomatic sample (N=520), where generalized anxiety symptoms correlated with the model's overgeneralization estimates. Simulations suggested that retrieval cues and cognitive interventions could prevent the return of fear, pointing to selective memory maintenance as a target for anxiety treatment.
papers.abstract: Return of fear after exposure poses a significant challenge for treatment of anxiety dis- orders. In this study, we used computational modeling to test competing mechanisms underlying spontaneous recovery of fear over time. We fit computational models of a novel theory of spontaneous recovery—selective maintenance of aversive memories— to behavior from a fear conditioning and extinction task (N=316), and showed that they uniquely captured spontaneous recovery and quantitatively outperformed alternative models embodying theories from the literature. The results were supported across mul- tiple datasets, including a preregistered replication (N=355) and a sample with mental health symptoms (N=520). The selective maintenance modeling framework addition- ally offers mechanistic insights into overgeneralization and the development of anxi- ety. Indeed, in the symptomatic sample we found that symptoms of generalized anxiety disorder correlated with estimates of overgeneralization in the model. Through simu- lations, we further demonstrated that insights from our model can explain how targeted interventions such as retrieval cues and cognitive interventions can prevent the return of fear. These results highlight selective maintenance of aversive events in memory as a critical and testable target for improving anxiety treatments and preventing relapse.

papers.title: Neural Racing Accumulator Model Estimation With Lightweight Monotonic Flows
papers.authors: Malte Lüken, Stefan T. Radev, Lourens Waldorp et al.
papers.summary: The paper proposes a method for estimating parameters of race models of decision-making with intractable densities, by training a small neural network with a monotonic neural spline flow to learn each runner's probability and cumulative density functions. This yields efficient likelihoods usable with modern samplers and decouples training from the choice of prior or parameterization. The authors demonstrate it on tractable and intractable versions of the racing diffusion model and argue that lightweight neural density estimators are advantageous when such flexibility is needed.
papers.abstract: Race models describe speeded decision-making as a race between competing runners that accumulate evidence in favor of available choice options. Their parameters can be estimated through the model likelihood that combines the probability and cumulative density functions of each runner. However, estimating parameters of complex race models whose runners have intractable densities with (hierarchical) Bayesian inference has been challenging: Numerical density approximations tend to be slow and amortized neural posterior estimation methods require complex network architectures that can be expensive to train and, in classical settings, tie the trained estimator to a specific prior distribution and generative model. We propose a flexible neural estimation method that decouples training from the choice of prior distribution or model parameterization. We train a small neural network together with a monotonic neural spline flow to simultaneously learn the runners' conditional probability density and cumulative density functions. We then combine both functions to efficiently estimate race model likelihoods that can be used in combination with modern samplers. We demonstrate the utility of our approach on both tractable and intractable versions of the popular racing diffusion model. Based on our results, we argue that, when flexibility in choosing prior distributions or model parameterizations is needed, learning the model likelihood with lightweight neural density estimators is advantageous.

papers.title: fMRI hyperscanning reveals widespread neural coupling during natural conversations
papers.authors: Laetitia Mwilambwe-Tshilobo, Lily Tsoi, Sebastian Speer et al.
papers.summary: Dyads were scanned simultaneously with fMRI during free-flowing conversation and during a control in which they read aloud another dyad's scripted dialogue, preserving turn-taking but removing co-construction. Natural conversation produced widespread intersubject neural alignment across regions tied to attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition. Speakers and listeners also anticipated each other within a short window, with activity in the same systems preceding the partner's. The findings suggest live, co-constructed conversation aligns brains beyond passive or scripted communication.
papers.abstract: Conversation is one of the most powerful tools that people have for building and maintaining social connections. How does conversation bring two minds together? Here we tracked the neural dynamics between dyads during real-time conversation using fMRI hyperscanning, where both people were scanned simultaneously, to explore whether and how conversation aligns brains. Dyads engaged in natural, free-flowing conversation as they co-constructed the content of their dialogue. In a control condition, partners read aloud scripted dialogue from another dyad’s conversation, preserving the turn-taking structure while removing the co-construction. To examine neural alignment, we compared whole-brain intersubject correlation between partners in each condition, assessing both synchronous and predictive neural dynamics. Results showed that naturalistic conversation led to significant widespread neural alignment across brain regions implicated in attention, audition, affect, executive control, and social cognition, compared to scripted conversation. Temporally refined analyses showed that during naturalistic conversation, relative to scripted conversation, both speakers and listeners anticipated each other within a short temporal window, with brain activity preceding their partner’s in the same neural systems. These findings show that live, turn-taking conversations align neural activity well beyond passive or asynchronous communication, providing a foundation for future research examining how spontaneous, co-constructed dialogue allows people to communicate effectively.

papers.title: Do bilinguals avoid ambiguity or minimise processing effort? Insights from an online eye-tracking study in spoken Mandarin
papers.authors: Yajun Liu, Antonella Sorace, Kenny Smith
papers.summary: Two spoken Mandarin experiments, a picture naming task and a version with online WebGazer eye-tracking, tested whether bilinguals avoid ambiguity generally or only when doing so reduces cognitive load. Contrary to the general ambiguity-avoidance hypothesis, Mandarin-English bilinguals in the UK used ambiguous expressions more often than more-monolingual speakers in China. Bilinguals directed early attention to image pairs with more accessible labels, while more-monolinguals monitored ambiguity depending on their responses. The authors interpret this as support for effort minimisation and as relevant to bilingual lexical access and early lexical attrition.
papers.abstract: Previous research shows that bilinguals tend to choose more explicit referential forms (e.g., overt pronouns over null pronouns) compared to monolingual speakers, but the mechanisms driving this tendency remain debated. By conducting two experiments examining lexical ambiguity in spoken Mandarin, we tested two hypotheses: Hypothesis 1: bilinguals would rather be redundant than ambiguous in general; Hypothesis 2: bilinguals avoid ambiguity only when doing so helps reduce cognitive load. In Experiment 1, L1 Mandarin L2 English speakers in the UK and more-monolingual speakers in China completed a picture naming task, where we manipulated whether the context in which a picture is named makes the preferred label ambiguous (e.g., do speakers avoid saying “fen3 si1” when describing a picture of glass noodles when it appears alongside a picture of fans which shares the same label?). Experiment 2 extended this task by incorporating online eye-tracking using WebGazer. Our results showed that, contrary to Hypothesis 1, bilinguals were more likely than more-monolinguals to use ambiguous expressions. Eye-tracking analysis revealed that bilinguals tended to direct early attention toward image pairs with more accessible labels, indicating a preference for linguistic choices that are cognitively less demanding; by contrast, more-monolinguals showed proactive monitoring of ambiguity depending on their responses. These findings support Hypothesis 2 and shed light on cognitive constraints in bilingual lexical access and early signs of lexical attrition.

papers.title: srifm: Role of lexical information for perceptual learning
papers.authors: Alejandrina Cristia, Annika Hultén, Holger Mitterer
papers.summary: The abstract describes using perceptual learning to test predictions of lexical feedback models such as TRACE against autonomous models such as Shortlist and Merge. It notes that listeners rapidly learn novel pronunciations of phonemic categories after about 10 ambiguous instances in unambiguous words. The abstract is cut off before any methods or results are given, so the findings are not reported.
papers.abstract: Linguistic representations continue to be updated, probably implicitly, as a side effect of normal language use. In particular, a large body of work shows that we learn novel pronunciations of well-established phonemic categories rapidly (Norris, McQueen, &amp; Cutler, 2003). This learning is thought to be automatic, such that it operates quickly once there is sufficient information to disambiguate the identity of that novel pronunciation: Effects are seen after encountering 10 instances of the ambiguous sound within unambiguous lexical items. Here, we uses perceptual learning to test predictions from two types of theories of speech perception, lexical feedback models (e.g., TRACE, McClelland &amp; Elman, 1986; Magnuson et al., 2003) and autonomous models (e.g., Shortlist, Norris, 1994; Merge, McQueen &amp; Cutler, 2010). According to TRACE, phonemes, and words are tracked in the input in parallel, and decisions at both of these levels are influenced online by the other levels. In this model, disambiguation is driven by the lexical level. In contrast, Merge postulates that listeners accumulate knowledge of sublexical representations, such as diphone probabilities, in addition to lexical knowledge.
